ruleIntents.intent: The rule computes, for every visible text character, the HIGHEST POSSIBLE contrast ratio between its foreground color(s) and background color(s), and checks that ratio against the WCAG AAA "enhanced" contrast thresholds (4.5:1 for large-scale text, 7.0:1 for everything else). It works from computed CSS color + background (solid, gradient, background image, alpha/opacity-composited, shadow-DOM, user-agent defaults), takes the best-case pixel pairing as the contrast value, and exempts text that is purely decorative or does not express anything in human language. It only computes contrast for text that is actually rendered/visible and is a text-node child of an HTML element.
ruleIntents.scLimb: This rule is mis-tagged in the harness header (`requirements(in-scope): 1.4.3`). By its own Rule Mapping, Expectation thresholds (4.5:1 large / 7.0:1 normal), and Requirements Mapping, it primarily tests 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) AAA — the STRICTER enhanced-contrast limb. For SC 1.4.3 specifically it only exercises the limb indirectly and over-strictly: it touches 1.4.3's core "visual presentation of text and images of text has a contrast ratio of at least X" requirement, and its exceptions limb (incidental/decorative text, disabled/inactive UI components, text that conveys no human language). It does NOT use 1.4.3's actual thresholds (3:1 large / 4.5:1 normal), and 1.4.3 is declared a secondary requirement that "is less strict than this rule," so some of this rule's FAILED examples can still PASS 1.4.3. It does not touch 1.4.3's logos/brand-name exception (declared an assumption/out of scope here) or the incidental-text "pure decoration" carve-out beyond the human-language test.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any visible character in a text node that is a child (in the flat tree) of an HTML element. Excluded: text under a disabled inheriting semantic group/widget; text used in the accessible name of a disabled inheriting semantic widget; non-visible text (display:none, off-screen positioning, foreground == background color so contrast is 1:1); text that is not in a text node (e.g. an img inside a p); and text not parented by an HTML element (e.g. SVG <text>).
ruleIntents.expectation: For each applicable text target, the highest possible contrast between foreground and background colors must be at least 4.5:1 for large-scale text and 7.0:1 for other text. Exempt from the threshold: text that is purely decorative, or text that does not express anything in a human language (e.g. an "X" glyph used as a close-button icon with aria-label). Note these are AAA (1.4.6) thresholds; passing implies likely 1.4.3 conformance, but failing does NOT necessarily mean 1.4.3 is violated.

Background-image backgrounds (black-hole.jpeg) with text-shadow, pass and fail
Alpha/transparency: rgba foreground alpha, CSS opacity on the element, and semi-transparent text over a split black/white background (color compositing)
User-agent default colors: no styles (black/white 21:1), default link color #0000EE, default role=button text
Shadow DOM: text inside an attached shadow root, pass and fail
Human-language exemption: 'X' close button (no language) passes regardless of contrast; Helvetica example proves informative text is not 'decorative'
Native vs ARIA semantics parity: <button> vs <div role=button>, and disabled <button> vs role=button aria-disabled
Disabled-widget / disabled-label inapplicability: label-for-disabled-input, aria-labelledby of aria-disabled textbox, disabled fieldset, role=group aria-disabled
Non-applicable text nodes: SVG text, img-only paragraph, display:none, off-screen, foreground==background (1:1)
syntheticNarrowness: WRONG SC ENTIRELY for the harness's purpose: every threshold and pass/fail boundary is calibrated to AAA 1.4.6 (7.0:1 / 4.5:1), not AA 1.4.3 (4.5:1 / 3:1). Cases failing here (e.g. 5.7:1, 6.4:1 contrast) actually PASS 1.4.3, so using this rule's failures as 1.4.3 ground truth would mislabel conforming pages as violations.

All targets are single short ASCII strings ('Some text in English', 'My button!', 'Black hole sun') in tiny isolated documents; no real paragraphs, mixed inline styling, nested spans with different colors, or list/table/form layouts.

No real font-size variety near the large-text boundary beyond exactly 18pt / 14pt-bold; no sub-pixel/rendered-size ambiguity, no rem/em/zoom/viewport-relative sizing, no font-weight gradations that affect the large-text classification.

Backgrounds are toy: one solid color, one two-stop linear gradient, or one specific JPEG. No real-world photographic hero images, CSS multiple-background stacks, semi-transparent overlays on imagery, fixed/parallax backgrounds, video backgrounds, or backgrounds painted by ancestor elements far up the tree.

Color is always explicitly inline or pure UA default; no cascade conflicts, CSS custom properties, dark-mode/prefers-color-scheme media queries, :hover/:focus/:visited state colors, or theme toggles that change contrast at runtime.

State coverage is shallow: only static initial render. No focus/hover/active/selected/placeholder/error states, no scrolled position over a different background, no carousel/animation frames where text crosses contrasting regions.

The decorative / human-language exemption is tested only via one icon glyph ('X') and one font-specimen sentence; no emoji, no Unicode symbol fonts, no pseudo-content (::before icons), no decorative dropcaps, no watermark text, no real ambiguity about whether text 'expresses human language'.
Logos/brand-name exception (a real 1.4.6 AND 1.4.3-incidental carve-out) is explicitly NOT exercised — assumed handled as images — so the corpus never tests text-based logotypes.
Transparency cases are clean two-color composites; no stacked alpha layers, blend-modes (mix-blend-mode), backdrop-filter, or anti-aliased edge pixels that real renderers produce.
Shadow DOM and native-vs-ARIA parity are each shown once with trivial markup; no slotted content, nested shadow roots, or custom elements with complex styling.

Single-browser/single-render assumption baked in (the rule itself flags CSS-support and Presentational-Roles-Conflict variance); the synthetic cases never reflect cross-browser rendering differences that change which background a character sits on.

ruleIntents.intent: For every visible text character, it computes the HIGHEST POSSIBLE foreground-to-background contrast ratio (the best-case over the text's pixel range — e.g. across a gradient, background image, text-shadow, or split background) and checks that best case clears the WCAG threshold: 3.0:1 for large-scale text, 4.5:1 for everything else. It deliberately uses the most favorable contrast, so a pass means "not guaranteed to fail" rather than "definitely legible." Text that conveys nothing in human language, is purely decorative, or belongs to a disabled widget/label is excluded.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The core 1.4.3 quantitative threshold limb: "visual presentation of text ... has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, except for Large Text [3:1]." It also exercises the SC's exception limb (Incidental: inactive UI components, decorative, not visible to anyone) via the disabled-ancestor/disabled-label applicability carve-outs and the purely-decorative/non-human-language expectation carve-out. It does NOT cover the Logotypes exception (explicitly assumed away) nor the 1.4.6 enhanced threshold.

Variable / gradient background ('highest possible contrast' / least-favorable-pixel limb): linear-gradient white-to-blue passes when worst point still >=4.5 (PE2) and fails when worst point drops to ~1.2:1 (FE2).
Background-image contrast (technique F83 territory): text over black-hole.jpeg passes at 13:1..5:1 (PE3) and fails at 2.7:1..3:1 (FE3).
Text-shadow affecting effective contrast: white shadow raising legibility (PE4) and grey shadow lowering it to 2.7-2.9:1 (FE11).
Alpha / opacity reducing effective foreground luminance: rgba(0,0,0,.3) FAIL (FE4) and opacity:.3 on the text element FAIL (FE5) — the computed-color vs nominal-color limb of the contrast definition.
Split / two-region background where one region fails (semi-transparent text over black|white split, 2.3:1..4.2:1) — FE7.
'visual presentation of text' definition limb — 1:1 same-color text is treated as NOT visual presentation, hence inapplicable (IE3, color:white on white).

Decorative / 'does not express anything in human language' exception — PASS for an aria-label=Close button whose visible content is 'X' (PE7); and the counter-case that informative prose in a decorative-looking font is NOT decorative and must pass/fail on its merits (FE8).

Also the contrast-side: an ENABLED button/role=button at 3.85:1 FAILS (FE9, FE10).

aspects.title: Pure-decoration exemption misjudged: genuinely decorative low-contrast text (must be EXEMPT) vs. meaningful text the author treated as decoration (must MEET contrast)
aspects.description: SC 1.4.3 exempts text that is 'pure decoration' / 'decorative and conveys no information.' Understanding's test is semantic: text is decorative only if 'random words... could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning.' Trusted Tester says to EXCLUDE text that is 'purely decorative and not meaningful (no functionality).' Deciding whether a faint watermark, ghost number, or faded divider conveys information is a meaning judgment a contrast checker cannot make. Two opposite human-judgment traps exist: (1) FALSE POSITIVE — genuine decoration (a mood word, an ornamental repeating glyph) flagged as a failure when it should be exempt; (2) FALSE NEGATIVE — core information (a price, a status watermark) styled faint and 'subtle' that the author rationalizes as decorative but which carries meaning and must meet 4.5:1/3:1. An automated checker sees only the failing ratio in both directions and cannot tell which way to rule.
aspects.scLimb: Pure-decoration / 'decorative and conveys no information' exemption (the meaning-vs-ornament judgment), distinct from the human-language glyph test ACT already covers.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus exercises the exemption only via a single non-language glyph ('X' close button) and a single font specimen. It has no case where meaningful prose is rendered at failing contrast yet styled to read as decoration (watermark, ghost step-number, hero mood word), and no case that must be EXEMPTED as genuine decoration. Neither the false-positive nor the false-negative side of the meaning boundary is tested, and no automated checker can resolve it because both produce identical failing ratios.

references.quote: Text that is decorative and conveys no information is excluded. For example, if random words are used to create a background and the words could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning, then it would be decorative and would not need to meet this criterion.
EXCLUDE text that is: ... Purely decorative and not meaningful (no functionality)

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages with live HTML text at clearly-failing contrast (2-3:1) where the markup gives the checker no way to know the meaning. Pair decorative-and-exempt cases against information-styled-as-decorative cases using near-identical markup so the only differentiator is semantic content. Use CSS to make text faint (light gray on white, low-opacity overlays). The judge must read the words and the surrounding layout to decide whether removal/substitution changes meaning.
suggestedScenarios: A faded gray repeating 'DRAFT' watermark across a contract at ~1.6:1 that conveys document status — meaningful, must NOT be exempted as decoration even though tools see only failing contrast.

A hero banner with a giant pale word 'INSPIRE' over a photo purely as a mood flourish whose removal/substitution changes nothing — genuinely decorative, should be EXEMPT, but a contrast checker flags it.
A pricing card whose key number '$49' is light-gray-on-white at ~2.8:1 because the designer called it a 'subtle accent' — core information wrongly styled as decorative; must meet contrast.
A section divider made of a faint repeating word ('· menu · menu · menu ·') used purely as an ornamental rule between sections — decorative, should be exempt.

Faint ghost numbers '01 02 03' behind feature cards as pure styling (decorative, exempt) vs. the same faint numbers being the ONLY visible step indicators of a wizard (meaningful, must meet contrast) — identical visuals, opposite verdicts.
A pull-quote duplicating body text set in pale italic at ~3.2:1 'for style' — requires judging whether the repetition adds meaning beyond the body text.

aspects.title: Logotype / brand-name contrast exemption and its loss when the logotype acts as an interactive UI component
aspects.description: 1.4.3 exempts logotypes and brand names from contrast. Trusted Tester excludes 'text that is... In logotypes (logo or brand name).' Understanding warns the exemption 'can be problematic when logos or logotypes act as user interface components (such as a link or other interactive control)' and that 'Corporate identity or brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are not included in the exception.' Three human judgments are required and none are automatable: (a) is this low-contrast text actually a logotype/brand wordmark versus an ordinary styled heading?; (b) is the wordmark functioning as a live control (home link, button), in which case the brand exemption is eroded and a sufficient-contrast variant is expected?; (c) is adjacent text (tagline, badge) being smuggled under the logo exemption when it is really informative content the brand carve-out does not cover?
aspects.scLimb: Logotype/brand-name exemption — including its erosion when the logo is an interactive control, and the boundary that brand guidelines beyond the logo are not exempt. ACT declares this entire limb out of scope.
aspects.whyUncovered: The 09o5cg rule lists logos/brand names explicitly as an assumption / out of scope; the corpus contains zero logotypes, wordmarks, or low-contrast brand-name links. So neither the legitimate exemption, nor its erosion when the logo is a link, nor the 'beyond the logo' boundary is exercised. An automated checker cannot identify what is a brand name versus a styled heading, so this is irreducibly human.

references.quote: Text used as part of a logo or logotype is exempted from contrast requirements... However, this can be problematic when logos or logotypes act as user interface components (such as a link or other interactive control). In these cases, as a best practice, authors should consider choosing a variant of the logo or logotype that has sufficient text contrast
Corporate identity or brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are not included in the exception.
EXCLUDE text that is: In logotypes (logo or brand name)

aspects.constructionStrategy: Render brand names as live HTML text (not images) at deliberately low contrast (brand pale-teal/pale-gold on white, ~2.2:1) so the contrast checker fires. Vary the role: bare wordmark in a header (exempt), wordmark wrapped in <a href='/'> (eroded exemption), pale heading that merely looks like a wordmark but is an article title (not exempt), and a tagline/badge adjacent to the logo (not covered by the exemption). The judge must reason about identity and function, not pixels.
suggestedScenarios: A site header whose company wordmark 'acmecorp' is live HTML text in brand pale-teal on white at ~2.2:1 — exempt as a logotype, must NOT be failed.
The same 'acmecorp' wordmark wrapped in <a href='/'> as the home link at ~2.2:1 — now a UI component; the brand exemption is questionable and a sufficient-contrast variant is expected.
A pale-gold 'GOLDLEAF' that LOOKS like a brand wordmark but is actually the article title (an <h1>) — must NOT get the logo exemption; only meaning distinguishes it.
A footer tagline 'Beyond the brand.™' rendered low-contrast and claimed as 'brand identity' — brand guidelines beyond logo/logotype are not exempt, so it must meet contrast.
A sponsor strip of six low-contrast partner brand names, several wrapped as links to sponsors — mixed exemption status across one row.
A nav where the brand wordmark passes contrast but an adjacent low-contrast 'BETA' badge is really a status label (not part of the logo) that must meet contrast.

aspects.title: Inactive-UI exemption applies only to GENUINELY inoperable controls, not to operable controls merely styled to look disabled (or aria-disabled controls that still fire)
aspects.description: Inactive UI components are exempt: Understanding says 'User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction... are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable.' Trusted Tester excludes text 'For inactive (disabled) user interface components.' Whether the exemption applies depends on a BEHAVIORAL fact — is the control actually operable? — that contrast checkers (and even most automated tools) cannot infer from color alone. The trap is appearance/behavior mismatch: a button greyed to look disabled (class='disabled', no disabled attr) that still submits on click MUST meet contrast; conversely a control marked aria-disabled='true' but wired to still fire is not genuinely inactive. The judge must drive the control to determine operability, then decide the exemption.
aspects.scLimb: Inactive (disabled) UI-component exemption — specifically the boundary where visual disabled-styling diverges from actual operability. ACT only tests correctly-marked genuinely-disabled widgets.
aspects.whyUncovered: All ACT inapplicable cases use correctly-marked disabled/aria-disabled native widgets that ARE inert. There is no operable control dressed to look disabled (faux-disabled, must MEET contrast), and no aria-disabled control that still fires. The exemption boundary is never stressed by mismatched appearance vs. behavior, and resolving it requires interacting with the page, which static checkers do not do.

references.quote: User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction (e.g., a disabled control in HTML) are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable.
An example would be a submit button at the bottom of a form that is visible but cannot be activated until all the required fields in the form are completed.
EXCLUDE text that is: For inactive (disabled) user interface components

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build controls whose visual treatment (grey, low-contrast, ~2.5:1) does not match their behavior. Include inline JS handlers (onclick) or tabindex+keydown so the 'disabled-looking' control actually fires, and pair each against a genuinely disabled twin (native disabled attr) at the same contrast. The judge must determine operability (click/Enter) before ruling on the exemption. Keep everything self-contained with no network calls.
suggestedScenarios: A 'Submit' button greyed to ~2.5:1 with class='disabled' but NO disabled attribute and an onclick that still submits — operable, must MEET contrast.
A custom <div role='button' tabindex='0'> styled pale grey to imply disabled, still responding to Enter/click — exemption does not apply.
A toolbar of icons where two are aria-disabled='true' (genuinely inert, exempt) and one merely LOOKS dimmed but fires — identical visuals, different exemption status.
A 'Next' wizard button low-contrast and TRULY disabled (disabled attr) until a form validates — legitimately exempt; pairs against the faux-disabled case.
A pagination control where the dimmed current page (aria-current, not a target) is exempt-irrelevant, while a greyed-out 'Previous' link on page 1 is actually a working link — only one is in scope.
A grey 'Add to cart' that looks disabled but processes clicks and never communicated a disabled state to AT — operable, must meet contrast.

aspects.title: Determining the EFFECTIVE background behind text when color and background come from different tree levels, inherited cascade, z-indexed overlays, or composited semi-transparent layers (F24 cascade limb)
aspects.description: F24 fails content when a foreground color is specified without a guaranteed background (or vice versa) and stresses that 'It is not necessary that the foreground and background colors both be defined on the same element. Foreground text color is inherited from ancestor elements. If an element's background color has not been defined, the element will have a transparent background, so authors need to ensure that at least one of the element's ancestors has a defined background color.' Color may be set 'at any level in the cascade... by external stylesheets or through inheritance.' Determining what actually renders behind the glyphs — which ancestor's background, which z-indexed sibling overlay, which composited semi-transparent scrim — requires reasoning about the rendered layer stack, not the element's own declared background. This is exactly where naive CSSOM contrast tools mislabel: they read the element's local background (often transparent) and either skip the text or assume white, producing false passes/false negatives. The least-contrast judgment must be made against the REAL composited backdrop.
aspects.scLimb: F24 cascade/inheritance/compositing limb — figuring out the effective background behind text across the tree and through stacked translucent layers, the part F24 calls the hard case.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT case sets color and background together inline on the same element, or relies on UA defaults. No case has color inherited from a distant ancestor while the visible backdrop comes from a different ancestor, a z-indexed overlay, a translucent scrim composited over a photo, or a CSS multiple-background stack. Naive automated checkers structurally mis-handle these (they read the local background), so determining the true backdrop is a human visual/structural judgment.

references.quote: It is not necessary that the foreground and background colors both be defined on the same element. Foreground text color is inherited from ancestor elements. If an element's background color has not been defined, the element will have a transparent background, so authors need to ensure that at least one of the element's ancestors has a defined background color.
Color and background color may be specified at any level in the cascade of preceding selectors, by external stylesheets or through inheritance rules.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Construct pages where the text's color is inherited several levels up and the nearest declared background is on a non-parent layer. Use position:absolute overlays, z-index stacking, rgba scrims, CSS multiple backgrounds (gradient over photo), and dark-themed ancestors. Make the local element background transparent so a naive checker would read white. The judge must visually determine the composited backdrop behind the glyphs and apply the least-contrast threshold against it. Keep all images local (no network egress).
suggestedScenarios:
A card with color:#888 on the

, transparent card, white section, but a position:absolute dark hero image on shows through a gap so the real backdrop behind the text is the dark image — contrast must be judged against the dark layer.
Text in a translucent overlay (rgba(255,255,255,0.4)) sitting on a local photo; the rendered backdrop is the overlay composited over the photo, which a local-background reader will not compute.
CSS multiple backgrounds: background: linear-gradient(rgba(0,0,0,.6),rgba(0,0,0,.6)), url(photo.jpg) — the gradient scrim is the real backdrop, not the photo or the gradient alone.
Foreground inherited from body{color:#777}; the nearest ancestor with a background is <html> set to a dark theme color — contrast must be #777-vs-dark, not the default-white assumption.
A modal whose dialog has no background; the dimmed backdrop plus the underlying page both show through the semi-transparent dialog, contributing to the effective contrast behind the text.
A sticky low-contrast header overlapping different-colored sections as the page is judged at a scrolled position so the effective backdrop differs from the top-of-page render.

aspects.title: Background-image text where worst-case pixels behind SOME letters fail (least-contrast / per-letter) even though best-case or average contrast passes (F83)
aspects.description: F83 fails text over a background image when 'there is not sufficient contrast between the background image and the text' such that 'features of the background image can be confused with the text.' Its procedure requires the Quickcheck against the most-confusable region and, if that fails, checking 'the background behind each letter.' Trusted Tester operationalizes this: the human eyedroppers 'a pixel that provides the LEAST contrast' for both foreground and background. The ACT rule does the OPPOSITE — it takes the highest-possible (best-case) pixel pairing — so a photographic background that is mostly dark (text passes) but has a bright patch crossing three letters (those letters fail) is precisely the F83 failure the best-case algorithm structurally CANNOT flag. Catching it requires per-letter visual inspection over a real, high-variance image, exactly the harness's least-contrast pixel path.
aspects.scLimb: F83 background-image limb evaluated by the least-contrast / per-letter method — the inverse of ACT's best-case pixel scoring, and the canonical 'F looks like E' confusion.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT background cases use one toy JPEG (black-hole.jpeg) plus text-shadow tuned to pass/fail cleanly, and the rule scores BEST-case contrast. There is no real photographic background with high luminance variance where a small bright/dark patch crosses only some letters. The best-case algorithm reports pass; only a per-letter least-contrast visual check finds the failing letters — an irreducibly visual human task.

references.quote: When there is not sufficient contrast between the background image and the text, features of the background image can be confused with the text making it difficult to accurately read the text.
If the Quickcheck is false, then check to see if the background behind each letter has sufficient contrast with the letter.
select the Foreground color-dropper, click a pixel in the text font. If the text color is varied, choose a pixel that provides the least contrast.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Author pages with text over LOCAL high-variance photographic or textured backgrounds (sunset, foliage, marble veining, alternating tiles) where most of the image gives passing contrast but a localized region crosses only some letters and drops below 4.5:1 (or 3:1 for large text). Position the text precisely so the failing region intersects specific glyphs. The judge must eyedropper the least-contrast pixels per letter. Keep all images local to avoid network egress.
suggestedScenarios: White headline over a sunset photo dark on the left (passes) with a bright sky on the right where the last word washes out below 4.5:1 — only the trailing word fails.
Dark caption over a marble-texture image with thin pale veins running behind some letters, mimicking F83's 'lines cross behind letters' confusion.
A black product name over foliage: most leaves are dark (best-case passes) but a sunlit gap behind two letters drops contrast below threshold.
Light text over a portrait where the subject's white shirt sits behind the middle of the line, locally failing while dark-hair regions pass.
Menu text over a repeating tile background whose tiles alternate light/dark so every other character has insufficient contrast.
A large headline where text-shadow rescues contrast over the dark third of the image but is insufficient over the bright third — partial-letter failure.

aspects.title: Applying the correct AA thresholds (4.5:1 normal / 3:1 large) and the human large-text-size determination, where ACT only scored the stricter AAA limits
aspects.description: SC 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large-scale text (>=18pt or >=14pt bold). The ACT 09o5cg rule is calibrated to the AAA 1.4.6 thresholds (7:1 / 4.5:1), so cases it FAILS (e.g. 5.7:1, 6.4:1) actually PASS 1.4.3. Correctly judging 1.4.3 requires (a) applying the right AA threshold, and (b) deciding whether text qualifies as 'large-scale,' which Understanding notes is not a clean pixel cutoff: '18 point and bold can both have different meanings in different fonts but, except for very thin or unusual fonts, they should be sufficient,' anti-aliasing of 'particularly thin or unusual fonts' can render text 'with a much fainter color than the actual text color,' and font size must be 'obtained from the user agent or calculated on font metrics.' The threshold band between 3:1 and 4.5:1 is where the size classification flips the verdict — a human judgment about whether the rendered font is genuinely large-scale (and not a thin/unusual face that should not get the relaxed ratio).
aspects.scLimb: 1.4.3's actual AA thresholds (4.5:1 / 3:1) and the large-scale-text classification (font weight/family/rendered-size judgment near the boundary), neither of which ACT's AAA-calibrated rule exercises.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT only tests exactly 18pt and 14pt-bold at the AAA boundaries; it never tests the 1.4.3 band where a ratio is between 3:1 and 4.5:1 (passes if large, fails if normal), nor thin/unusual/condensed fonts where the relaxed large-text ratio is arguably unsafe, nor rem/em/zoom/responsive sizing that changes rendered size. Resolving the size classification near the boundary is a human judgment Understanding explicitly says depends on font metrics and weight, not a fixed pixel rule.

references.quote: 18 point text or 14 point bold text is judged to be large enough to require a lower contrast ratio... '18 point' and 'bold' can both have different meanings in different fonts but, except for very thin or unusual fonts, they should be sufficient.

Due to anti-aliasing, particularly thin or unusual fonts may be rendered by user agents with a much fainter color than the actual text color defined in the underlying CSS. This can lead to situations where text has a contrast ratio that nominally passes the Success Criterion, but has a much lower contrast in practice.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages with text whose computed contrast falls in the 3:1-to-4.5:1 band, paired so the same ratio is rendered once as genuinely large-scale (24px/18pt, or 14pt bold) and once as normal-size — the verdict flips on size classification. Add thin/condensed/unusual font faces at large size to probe whether the relaxed 3:1 ratio is safe, and use rem/em/percentage/viewport sizing to make the rendered size ambiguous. The judge must determine large-scale status from font metrics and weight, then apply the AA threshold.
suggestedScenarios: Body text at 3.4:1 in 16px normal weight (FAILS 1.4.3 at 4.5:1) right beside a 24px heading at the same 3.4:1 (PASSES at 3:1) — verdict flips on size.
A 14pt heading set bold (3:1 applies, ~3.2:1 passes) vs. the same 14pt heading at normal weight (4.5:1 applies, fails) — weight changes the threshold.

A heading in a very thin/hairline font at 20pt and 3.1:1 — nominally large-scale and passing 3:1, but the thin strokes/anti-aliasing make it effectively much fainter; a human should question the relaxed ratio.
Text sized in rem/em with a page font-size that yields a rendered size straddling the 18px-vs-24px boundary — the large-scale determination is ambiguous and must be computed from metrics.
A condensed/unusual display font at 18pt where '18pt' renders visually smaller than a normal 18pt face — Understanding's 'different meanings in different fonts' caveat applies.
A ratio of exactly ~4.4:1 normal text — must not be rounded up to 4.5; Understanding says 4.499:1 does not meet the threshold, so it FAILS.

aspects.title: Contrast of text only present in non-initial states: placeholder, hover, keyboard focus, active, selected, and error states (and visited-link exclusion)
aspects.description: Understanding explicitly extends 1.4.3 to 'text in the page, including placeholder text and text that is shown when a pointer is hovering over an object or when an object has keyboard focus. If any of these are used in a page, the text needs to provide sufficient contrast.' F24's best-practice note lists 'text, link text, visited link text, link text with hover and keyboard focus.' Trusted Tester warns 'Some text may not initially be visible (appears on mouseover or focus). It must still conform to the contrast requirement wherever it occurs,' while excluding text 'Changed to indicate it is a visited link.' Evaluating these requires DRIVING the page into each state (hover, focus, type into a field, trigger an error) and judging whether the state is genuinely reachable — a behavioral exploration the static, initial-render ACT corpus never performs.
aspects.scLimb: State-dependent presentations of text (placeholder, hover, focus, active, selected, error) that the SC explicitly covers, plus the visited-link exclusion — none scored at static initial render.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT case is scored at static initial render with no interaction; there are no :hover/:focus/:active/::placeholder/aria-selected variants, no error-state styling, and no driven states. The state-coverage breadth Understanding and F24 explicitly demand is entirely absent, and discovering these states requires interacting with the page rather than reading static markup.

references.quote: This success criterion applies to text in the page, including placeholder text and text that is shown when a pointer is hovering over an object or when an object has keyboard focus. If any of these are used in a page, the text needs to provide sufficient contrast.
Best practice is to include all states of the text. For example, text, link text, visited link text, link text with hover and keyboard focus, etc.
Some text may not initially be visible (appears on mouseover or focus). It must still conform to the contrast requirement wherever it occurs.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Author self-contained pages where text passes contrast at initial render but a non-initial state drops it below threshold (or is only present in that state). Use ::placeholder, :hover, :focus, :active pseudo-classes, aria-selected styling, and a JS-driven error message. Include a visited-link case to confirm the visited-state exclusion is honored. The judge must drive each state (hover, tab, type, submit) and confirm the state is reachable before measuring contrast.
suggestedScenarios: A search input whose ::placeholder text is pale grey at ~2.6:1 while typed text passes — placeholder must meet contrast.
A nav link that is fine at rest but whose :hover color drops to ~3:1 against the same background — hover state fails.
A custom dropdown where the keyboard-:focus option label changes to a low-contrast highlight color, only visible on focus.
A form field whose JS-inserted error message ('Email is required') renders light-red on white at ~3.1:1, present only after a failed submit.
An aria-selected tab whose selected-state text color drops below 4.5:1 while unselected tabs pass.

A link whose :visited color is set very faint — must be EXCLUDED from the contrast requirement (Trusted Tester excludes visited-link styling), paired with a hover state on the same link that is in scope.

aspects.title: The 'text in a picture that contains significant other visual content' exemption vs. an image of text done purely to get a particular look (which is NOT exempt)
aspects.description: 1.4.3 exempts text 'that are part of a picture that contains significant other visual content.' Understanding explains the boundary: 'This exception is intended to separate pictures that have text in them from images of text that are done to replace text in order to get a particular look. Incidental text, such as in photographs that happen to include a street sign, are not included.' Trusted Tester excludes text 'Contained within a picture that contains significant other visual content' but requires testing 'an image of text alone (or an image with text and no other significant content)' against 4.5:1/3:1 using the eyedropper. Deciding whether a given image is a 'picture with significant other content' (exempt) versus an 'image of text' styled for look (in scope) is a holistic visual judgment about the image's purpose and composition — not something an automated checker (which cannot read text inside images at all) can do.
aspects.scLimb: The 'picture with significant other visual content' / incidental-text exemption and its boundary against images-of-text-for-look — a limb ACT does not test, requiring image-content judgment.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT never tests images-of-text at all (it only computes contrast for live text nodes), and certainly not the exemption boundary between an incidental-text photograph (exempt) and an image-of-text crafted for a particular look (in scope at 4.5:1/3:1). Automated checkers cannot read text inside raster images, so both the exemption and the in-scope image-of-text contrast check are human-only.

references.quote: This exception is intended to separate pictures that have text in them from images of text that are done to replace text in order to get a particular look.
Incidental text, such as in photographs that happen to include a street sign, are not included.
If the page contains an image of text alone (or an image with text and no other significant content), test the image of text with CCA

aspects.constructionStrategy: Embed LOCAL raster images and ask the judge to classify and then, where in scope, eyedropper contrast inside the image. Pair clearly-incidental-text photographs (exempt) against images-of-text-for-look (in scope, with sufficient or insufficient embedded contrast). Use a real headline rasterized as a PNG at low contrast (in scope, fails) versus a product photo that happens to include packaging text (exempt). Keep every asset local to avoid network egress; provide alt text appropriately so the case turns on image purpose, not alt presence.
suggestedScenarios: A marketing hero where the headline is a low-contrast PNG image-of-text done purely for a custom typeface — in scope, must meet 4.5:1 (or 3:1 if large), and here it fails.
A photograph of a city street that incidentally includes a low-contrast street-sign — incidental text in a picture with significant other content, EXEMPT.

A product packaging photo whose printed label text is low-contrast against the package — a picture with significant other visual content, exempt, paired against a pure image-of-text logo-style banner that is in scope.
An infographic saved as a single JPEG whose body labels are pale-on-pale (~2.5:1) — these are images of text replacing real text for look, in scope and failing.

A book-cover image showing a stylized low-contrast title within rich cover artwork (significant other content) — exempt — versus the same title set as an isolated image-of-text banner elsewhere on the page (in scope).
A large-scale image-of-text quote at ~3.2:1 where the human must also decide whether the rendered text is large-scale (3:1) before judging pass/fail.

pages.scenario: Legal document viewer renders a Master Services Agreement with a tiled, rotated, light-gray repeating word 'DRAFT' behind the prose at ~1.56:1. The repeated word states the contract's legal status (unexecuted draft, not the signed final); the themer treats it as decorative paper texture.
pages.mechanism: Meaningful status text styled as a decorative repeated-word background. 'DRAFT' (#cfcfcf on #ffffff = 1.56:1) conveys document status that cannot be rearranged or substituted ('FINAL','VOID') without changing meaning, so it is NOT pure decoration and must meet 4.5:1; at 1.56:1 it fails SC 1.4.3.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A checker can compute 1.56:1 but cannot rule on the exemption: the markup is indistinguishable from a genuine decorative repeated-word background (the Understanding doc's own decoration example), and some scanners suppress rotated/tiled layers as decorative chrome. Deciding 'DRAFT' carries non-substitutable legal status requires reading the word and reasoning about the document — semantic judgment no scanner performs.

citation.quote: Text that is decorative and conveys no information is excluded. For example, if random words are used to create a background and the words could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning, then it would be decorative and would not need to meet this criterion.

pages.scenario: Trail-running e-commerce hero banner layers a giant pale word 'INSPIRE' (white at 35% alpha, ~2.0-2.4:1 over an inline-SVG photo) behind the real headline as a pure mood flourish. The informative content (H1, subhead, CTA) is white-on-dark with text-shadow and passes.
pages.mechanism: FALSE-POSITIVE side of the exemption boundary: the giant 'INSPIRE' is aria-hidden, is not a heading or label, and can be substituted ('EXPLORE','WANDER') or removed with no change in meaning, so it is exempt decoration; its ~2:1 ratio does not fail 1.4.3. All genuinely informative text meets contrast, so the page passes.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/Lighthouse measure the ~2:1 ratio of the pale word and would report a contrast violation (or 'needs review' over the photo), but the correct verdict is PASS because the text is exempt decoration. Tools cannot read the word, judge it conveys no information, and confirm it is substitutable/removable — the exact semantic test the exemption hinges on — so they raise a false positive where a human must rule 'exempt'.

pages.scenario: SaaS pricing page renders each plan's price NUMBER ($19/$49/$99) in pale gray #a3a3a3 on white (2.52:1) as a 'subtle accent', while the surrounding '$', '/mo', 'Billed monthly' and feature list are dark and pass. The price magnitude — the most decision-critical value — is the only failing-contrast text.
pages.mechanism: FALSE-NEGATIVE side: core information styled to read as decorative. The digits are the actual price (19 vs 49 vs 99 are different offers) and cannot be substituted without changing meaning, so they are in scope. At 56px/800 the large-text 3:1 threshold applies but 2.52:1 fails even that.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Two traps stack: surrounding small text all passes so a node-sampling scanner sees mostly green, and the failing element is large-scale text which some tools down-weight. Even a perfect ratio computation cannot decide that the faint big numeral is the price (in-scope information) rather than an ornamental large numeral — recognizing it is core info requires understanding the page is a pricing table, a human semantic judgment.

citation.quote: Text that is decorative and conveys no information is excluded. For example, if random words are used to create a background and the words could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning, then it would be decorative and would not need to meet this criterion.

pages.scenario: Restaurant menu uses a faint repeated word ('menu · menu · menu ·') as a decorative ornamental rule between sections, #d2d2d2 on cream ~1.5:1. The real section names are the dark <h2> 'Entrées'/'Plats' directly beneath; all item names, descriptions and prices are dark and pass.
pages.mechanism: Genuine pure-decoration case structurally near-identical to case-01's repeated word but with opposite ruling. The divider conveys no information (section identity comes from the dark headings), is aria-hidden, and could be replaced by dots/stars or removed with no change in meaning, so it is exempt; its ~1.5:1 ratio does not fail 1.4.3.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse would compute ~1.5:1 for the divider and report a violation (false positive). They cannot read the repeated word, recognize it as ornament, verify it is substitutable/removable, and confirm the real section names are dark — the exemption is a semantic judgment. The near-identical markup to case-01 with the opposite correct verdict is exactly why no static rule can resolve this aspect.

pages.scenario: Patient-intake multi-step form uses big faint numerals '01 02 03' (#d0d0d0 on white = 1.54:1) as its step rail. There is NO other step cue — no per-step text label, no 'Step 2 of 3' string, no dots, no progress bar — so the numerals carry the step/progress information. The same visual is pure decoration when used as 'ghost numbers' behind feature cards.
pages.mechanism: Identical-visuals/opposite-verdict trap. Because no other element conveys step position or count, the numerals are the information ('you are on step 2 of 3') and cannot be substituted or removed without losing meaning, so they are in scope; at 1.54:1 (failing even the 3:1 large-text bar) they fail. The decorative twin behind labelled feature cards would be exempt.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The markup and failing ratio are identical to the decorative 'ghost numbers' pattern, so no static rule can separate the two — a checker measures 1.54:1 in both and cannot know that here the numeral is the only step cue versus there it is ornament behind a labelled card. Some scanners also discount large pale numerals as decorative chrome. Resolving it requires reading the layout and noting the absence of any other progress indicator.

pages.scenario: Invoice has a cancelled line item ($1,800 on-site implementation). The ONLY cancellation signal is a faint rotated 'VOID' stamp across the row, #cdb3b3 ~1.96:1. The row text is full-contrast and NOT struck through, the $1,800 amount is still printed, and the $3,360 total already excludes it — so without reading the stamp the charge looks live. The author treated the stamp as a stylistic overlay.
pages.mechanism: Status-bearing overlay word styled as a faded decorative stamp. 'VOID' conveys non-substitutable financial status (cannot swap for 'PAID' or remove without changing the invoice's meaning), so it is in scope; at 1.96:1 a contrast-impaired user cannot read it and is misled about what they owe — fails 1.4.3.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A checker computes 1.96:1 but cannot decide the exemption: the faint rotated word is visually and structurally identical to a purely decorative 'stamp' graphic designers add for flavor, and many scanners ignore absolutely-positioned rotated overlays as decorative chrome. Ruling it in-scope requires reading 'VOID', recognizing it as the only cancellation cue, and reconciling it against the still-printed $1,800 line and the $3,360 total — multi-step semantic reasoning no tool performs.

citation.quote: Text used as part of a logo or logotype is exempted from contrast requirements, under the assumption that logos/logotypes must comply with stricter color choices mandated by corporate identity or brand guidelines.

pages.scenario: Project-management SaaS app shell ('Linaro') renders its wordmark as live HTML text in brand 'mist' (#6ec3b6) on white at ~2.07:1, wrapped in <a href='/'> and acting as the ONLY home affordance (no separate Home item, no logo image). pages.mechanism: The low-contrast text (~2.07:1, verified) is a logotype that is acting as a user-interface component (the sole home link), so per the 1.4.3 Understanding note the brand exemption is eroded and 4.5:1 applies; no sufficient-contrast variant or equivalent control is provided, so a low-vision keyboard user faces an under-contrast operable home control.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner computes ~2.07:1 but cannot supply the reasoning that makes the flag correct: that 'Linaro' is the brand wordmark AND that it is here the only home control. citation.quote: However, this can be problematic when logos or logotypes act as user interface components (such as a link or other interactive control). In these cases, as a best practice, authors should consider choosing a variant of the logo or logotype that has sufficient text contrast, if allowed by the corporate identity or brand guidelines. Alternatively, authors should consider providing an equivalent user interface component which serves the same purpose and meets contrast requirements.

pages.scenario: Investigative-finance publication ('The Ledger') runs a feature whose <h1> is the single word 'GOLDLEAF' set in a gilt, spaced, all-caps display serif in pale gold (#cdb368) on white at ~2.05:1. pages.mechanism: The sub-4.5:1 text (~2.05:1, verified) is the document's main heading (an <h1>), not the page's logotype. pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <h1> is well-formed and its ~2.05:1 contrast is computable, so a scanner can flag it — but it cannot decide whether the flag should be SUPPRESSED under the logotype exemption. citation.quote: It is not necessary that the foreground and background colors both be defined on the same element. Foreground text color is inherited from ancestor elements. If an element's background color has not been defined, the element will have a transparent background, so authors need to ensure that at least one of the element's ancestors has a defined background color.

pages.scenario: Wellness/yoga hero with near-white text (#f3f6f4) on a translucent white 'frosted glass' overlay (rgba(255,255,255,0.4)) composited over a bright beach/sky photo; the composite is a pale panel, so the light text falls to ~1.1-1.6:1.
pages.mechanism: The text's nearest box-tree background is .frost, whose computed value is a translucent color over a background-image. The effective backdrop is rgba(255,255,255,0.4) composited over the bright photo, yielding a light panel on which near-white text is ~1.1-1.6:1 — far below 4.5:1. A foreground and a background are both declared, so this is not a bare F24 omission; it is a composited-backdrop misjudgment.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The text node's nearest background (.frost) is a translucent color over an image — there is no single solid background color to sample, and the true backdrop also includes the photo pixels under the scrim. Tools either skip the node as having an incomputable background or ignore the alpha and the photo; none composite rgba(255,255,255,0.4) over the brightest photo region to find the actual pale backdrop, which is the human visual judgment F24/F83 require for background images.

citation.quote: To satisfy Success Criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) and 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced), there must be sufficient contrast between the text and its background. For pictures, this means that there would need to be sufficient contrast between the text and those parts of the image that are most like the text and behind the text.

pages.scenario: News feature banner using CSS multiple backgrounds — a linear-gradient scrim listed first (painted on top) over a url(skyline.jpg) photo — where the gradient's top stop is near-white (rgba(255,255,255,0.35)), so over the bright sky region the near-white headline (#fbfaf6) is ~1.25:1.
pages.mechanism: The effective backdrop is the gradient's TOP stop composited over the brightest (upper-sky) region of the skyline photo, not the photo's dark buildings nor the gradient in isolation. A background is declared (the multiple backgrounds) and the headline color is declared, so the defect is which stacked layer renders behind the glyphs; the least-contrast region resolves to ~1.25:1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A CSSOM contrast tool encounters a background shorthand containing both a gradient and an image, cannot reduce it to a single solid color, and skips the contrast computation (or falls back to white, mis-passing the near-white text). No scanner resolves the layer order of a multiple-background stack and composites the gradient's top stop over the correct (brightest) photo region to pick the worst-case area behind the headline.

citation.quote: With background images, authors will need to check text contrast against the various colors of the background image that will be behind the text, and may also want to consider contrast when images are not displayed.

pages.scenario: Fintech dark-theme dashboard: dark theme set on the root (html{background:#14171c}), <body> sets no background and color:#777, and a summary card gives itself background:#6f6f6f without resetting text color, so the card paragraphs keep the inherited #777 on near-identical #6f6f6f (~1.12:1) while a sibling card stays legible.
pages.mechanism:
The failing #777 reaches .panel p purely by inheritance from (not on the

pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No element trips an F24 missing-background linter (<html> and .panel both declare backgrounds). Catching it requires recognizing <body> sets no background so the dark <html> is the canvas, applying each card's own declared background to the SAME inherited foreground, and refusing the white fallback.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal consent modal: a translucent 'glass' dialog panel (rgba(255,255,255,0.55) + backdrop-filter blur) over a light dim scrim (rgba(20,30,45,0.35)) over a bright white app, with muted consent body text (#8a93a0); the panel-over-dim-over-page composite is light, so the text lands at ~2.2:1.
pages.mechanism: The dialog has correct ARIA and a declared background, so nothing is missing; the failure is that the effective backdrop is a multi-layer alpha composite (55% white glass over 35% navy dim over the bright page) that resolves to a light panel, on which #8a93a0 muted text is ~2.2:1, below 4.5:1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A CSSOM tool reads .modal's background as a single rgba color and either ignores the alpha (treating it as near-solid white) or cannot flatten a translucent panel at all and skips. pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive checker mis-handles even this correct page: .menu has a transparent background, so a CSSOM walker finds none and either falls back to a white canvas (reporting off-white-on-white as a FALSE failure) or cannot reduce the multiple-background hero to one color and skips. citation.quote: First do a quick check to see if the contrast between the text and the area of the image that is darkest (for dark text) or lightest (for light text) meets or exceeds that required by the Success Criterion (1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) or 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced)). If the contrast meets or exceeds the specified contrast, then there is no failure.

citation.quote: This failure occurs when people with low vision are not able to read text that is displayed over a background image. When there is not sufficient contrast between the background image and the text, features of the background image can be confused with the text making it difficult to accurately read the text.

citation.quote: Text that is larger and has wider character strokes is easier to read at lower contrast. The contrast requirement for larger text is therefore lower.

pages.scenario: SaaS usage/billing dashboard (Meterly): two card 'eyebrow' headings at 14pt (18.7px) in the same gray (#8e8e8e on white = 3.28:1) differ only by font-weight — the first is bold (700), the second normal (400). Bold 14pt is large-scale (PASSES 3:1); normal-weight 14pt is not (FAILS 4.5:1). The threshold flips on weight alone.
pages.mechanism: 1.4.3's large-scale boundary is '>=18pt OR >=14pt bold'. At 14pt the bold heading qualifies for 3:1 (3.28 passes); the regular-weight heading at the same size/color does not qualify, so 4.5:1 applies and 3.28:1 fails. Requires reading computed font-weight and applying the weight-conditional large-scale rule.

The corpus's AAA-calibrated 09o5cg also wrongly FAILS the bold heading (AAA-large needs 4.5). Correct AA verdict needs font-weight off the computed style plus AA (not AAA) thresholds — a judgment the AAA-only rule never tests.

pages.scenario: Gallery exhibition page (Atrium — Liminal): the title is an ultra-thin hairline weight (font-weight:100) at 20pt (26.7px) in teal #3d6c6c on near-black #111 = 3.20:1. By pixel size it is large-scale and nominally passes 3:1, but the hairline strokes anti-alias to a much fainter effective color, so practical contrast is below 3:1 — the SC's thin/unusual-font caveat.
pages.mechanism: The relaxed 3:1 minimum assumes 'wider character strokes'. A 100-weight hairline violates that premise: anti-aliased thin stroke edges blend toward the dark background so the perceived foreground luminance is far closer to #111 than #3d6c6c implies, dropping effective contrast below 3:1. The face must be recognized as thin/unusual and the nominal pass treated as a practical failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/Lighthouse compute contrast from the declared CSS color (#3d6c6c) and background (#111), get 3.20:1, classify 26.7px as large, compare to 3:1, and report PASS. They have no model of stroke width or anti-aliasing and cannot see the fainter effective color the hairline renders. Understanding 1.4.3 explicitly flags this nominal-pass/practical-fail gap for thin or unusual fonts — a human-only judgment.

Due to anti-aliasing, particularly thin or unusual fonts may be rendered by user agents with a much fainter
            color than the actual text color defined in the underlying CSS. This can lead to situations where text has
            a contrast ratio that nominally passes the Success Criterion, but has a much lower contrast in practice.

This heading renders at 21px once the inherited 87.5% root is resolved, making it normal-size text held to 4.5:1, which 3.79:1 fails. The classification can only be made by computing rendered px from font metrics, as the SC requires.

The AAA-calibrated 09o5cg rule only tests fixed-pixel boundary text and never exercises rem/em-cascaded sizing where large-scale status depends on resolving an inherited root.

pages.scenario: Restaurant menu (Cantina del Molo): course headers ('Antipasti', 'Primi') use a condensed display face (font-stretch:condensed, Arial Narrow stack) at 24px (=18pt) in terracotta #9c5a30 on charcoal #141414 = 3.44:1. By pixel size it is large-scale and nominally passes 3:1, but the condensed face packs narrower glyphs so '18pt' covers far less ink than a normal 18pt face — Understanding's 'different meanings in different fonts' caveat.
pages.mechanism: The relaxed 3:1 ratio assumes ordinary faces 'larger and with wider character strokes'. A condensed face narrows glyphs and tightens counters so the effective size at 18pt is smaller than a normal 18pt face, removing the legibility cushion. The face should be recognized as unusual/condensed and not safely entitled to the relaxed ratio; held to 4.5:1, 3.44:1 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/Lighthouse classify large-scale by nominal pixel size (24px => large) and compute 3.44:1 vs the 3:1 threshold, returning PASS. They have no notion of font-stretch, glyph width, or x-height and cannot decide a condensed 18pt is effectively smaller than the relaxed ratio assumes. Understanding reserves the relaxed ratio for ordinary faces ('except for very thin or unusual fonts') — a font-metrics judgment requiring a human to view the rendered condensed type.

"18 point" and "bold" can both have different meanings in

pages.scenario: State DMV vehicle-registration form (Calverton DMV): the statutory privacy/fee disclosure is rendered in the agency 'fine print' slate #767880 at 16px normal weight on white = exactly 4.40:1. Normal-size text requires 4.5:1; 4.40 is a hair below and reads as 'basically 4.5' to a skimming reviewer, but Understanding says the ratios are thresholds and must not be rounded (4.499 does not meet 4.5).
pages.mechanism: The disclosure is normal-size body text, so the AA minimum is a hard 4.5:1 with no large-text relief. 4.40:1 is below the threshold; the ratio is a threshold value, not an approximation, so it is not rounded up. The correct judgment is to compare without rounding and fail.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A precise checker computes 4.40 < 4.5, so this is not a computation blind spot — it is the human disposition near the threshold: auditors routinely round near-threshold values ('4.4 is basically 4.5') and pass low-priority legal fine print, and some tools apply rounding/tolerance slack. Understanding 1.4.3 exists to settle exactly this, stating values 'should not be rounded'. The corpus's AAA-calibrated 09o5cg rule gives no reliable AA-threshold signal at the 4.5 boundary.

pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse compute contrast for DOM text nodes; a ::placeholder is generated content with no text node, so axe's color-contrast rule skips it. Every real text node (typed value, headings, prices) passes, so a static scan is all-green. A human must view the empty field, recognise the faint prompt as in-scope text, and measure placeholder-vs-field colour.

pages.scenario: Business-news masthead with a horizontal section nav. Links are dark brand blue (#1a3a6b, ~11.3:1) at rest, but :hover and :focus recolour them to a pale brand blue (#8aa4c8) on the same white bar (~2.55:1) for 15px normal-weight text.

pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners evaluate the static, un-hovered render; no pointer is over any element during a scan and they do not synthesize :hover/:focus, so they read the resting #1a3a6b (~11.3:1, passing). The :hover rule is real CSS that repaints the link, but a scanner never enters that state. Detecting it requires driving the page into hover/focus and re-measuring.

citation.quote: Best practice is to include all states of the text. For example, text, link text, visited link text, link text with hover and keyboard focus, etc.

pages.scenario: Cloud-console billing form with a custom APG listbox country picker driven by aria-activedescendant. Resting options are dark (#1d2733 on white, ~15:1). The keyboard-focused (active descendant) option gets a pale highlight: #9fb0c9 text on a #eef3fb fill (~1.98:1). As the user arrows down, the focused option's label is the hardest to read.
pages.mechanism: The active-option class .opt--active sets colour #9fb0c9 on background #eef3fb = ~1.98:1, below 4.5:1. This is text shown only when an object has keyboard focus — explicitly in scope — so the focused option's label fails contrast for every option as focus roves.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Contrast engines read each option's resting computed style (~15:1, passing) and cannot drive arrow-key navigation to move focus and re-measure the active descendant; in production the listbox is also hidden until opened, so a static initial-render scan never sees the options at all. Confirming the failure requires a human to open the list, arrow through it, and read each highlighted label.

pages.scenario: Bank money-transfer form. On load all text passes. Submitting with an empty amount makes JS inject an inline error 'Enter an amount to transfer.' styled light-red #e98a8a on white (~2.48:1). Long-tail twist: the submit button's label is fine at rest/hover but its :active (pressed) rule recolours the label to #a9c2e8 on the #2f6fd6 button (~2.65:1), unreadable while held down.
pages.mechanism: The injected error text (#e98a8a on #fff = ~2.48:1) and the pressed-state button label (#a9c2e8 on #2f6fd6 = ~2.65:1) both fall below 4.5:1. The error is in-scope state-dependent text present after a failed submit; the button is enabled (not the inactive-control exception), so its :active label is in scope too.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The error element does not exist in the DOM at load — scanners do not submit the form, so they have no node to evaluate. The :active label colour is only computed while the button is pressed, a state scanners never synthesize. Every text node at initial render passes and the markup is well-formed (labels, aria-live, aria-describedby), so naive checks are green. Catching either failure requires driving the page: submit empty and press-and-hold the button.

pages.scenario: Marketing-analytics app with an APG tablist (Overview, Channels, Audience, Spend). Unselected tabs are dark text (#283543 on #eef2f6, ~11.1:1) and pass. The selected tab gets a 'pill' treatment: white text on a pale-teal gradient (effective #9ad8d4, ~1.60:1). Selection roves, so whichever tab is selected inherits the failing white-on-pale-teal treatment.
pages.mechanism: [role=tab][aria-selected=true] paints white (#fff) text on a ~#9ad8d4 pill = ~1.60:1, below 4.5:1. The selected state is the in-scope presentation here; the SC requires contrast 'wherever it occurs', including state-dependent presentations, and the failure is a property of the selected state for every tab.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A static scan sees exactly one tab selected and the rest passing, and does not activate the other tabs to confirm each fails when selected. Many engines also treat the rounded gradient 'pill' as a component region and down-rank/skip its text rather than measuring white-on-pale-teal as a text-on-background pair. Establishing that the failure follows the selected STATE (true for any tab) requires driving the tablist and re-measuring per selection.

pages.scenario: University coursework-wiki reading list where already-opened links fade (the 'already read' marker). The :visited colour is deliberately faint (#b9b3c9 on white, ~2.03:1, below 4.5:1), but visited-link styling is on the SC's EXCLUDE list. All in-scope states pass: unvisited a:link (~12.1:1), :hover (~14.9:1), :focus-visible (~14.9:1 + outline). Boundary/PASS case that tests whether the judge honours the visited exclusion instead of over-flagging the driven low-contrast state.
pages.mechanism: No in-scope text is below threshold: rest/hover/focus link states all exceed 12:1. The only sub-threshold state is :visited (~2.03:1), and Trusted Tester explicitly excludes text 'Changed to indicate it is a visited link' from the contrast requirement, so the faint visited colour is not a 1.4.3 failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: For privacy, browsers never expose the real :visited colour via getComputedStyle and scanners do not synthesize a visited state, so tools never see the faint colour at all — they pass it only by accident of not measuring. The CORRECT human verdict (pass) rests on a judgment tools cannot make: recognising the faint colour is the visited state and that the visited-link exclusion removes it from scope, rather than flagging the measured ~2.03:1 after clicking a link.

problems: MINOR DOC INACCURACY (does not change outcome): the watermark is font-size:46px font-weight:700 = 34.5pt bold, which is WCAG 'large text', so the applicable 1.4.3 threshold is 3:1, NOT the 4.5:1 stated in case-01.md (lines 33-34) and the HTML comment (line 112). The text still fails the correct 3:1 large-text threshold at 1.56:1, so the 'failed' outcome stands, but the rationale cites the wrong required ratio.
The .md and HTML comment repeatedly assert 'must meet 4.5:1'; for this large bold text the precise requirement is 3:1. Recommend correcting the threshold wording for accuracy, not dropping the case.

Cosmetic prompt/page drift: the orchestration prompt describes the flourish as 'INSPIRE' at '35% alpha', but the actual HTML (line 83) and the .md both use the word 'WANDER' at color rgba(255,255,255,.30) (30% alpha). The HTML and .md are internally consistent; only the prompt's framing string is stale. Not a page defect.

The 'tools false-positive' narrative is partially overstated for axe-core specifically: axe-core SKIPS aria-hidden=true text for color-contrast and would therefore pass silently rather than raise a false positive. The doc hedges adequately ('or report needs-review when sampling over the photo') and the cited trusted-tester ANDI/CCA manual flow WOULD surface the faint word as a 'Manual Contrast Test Needed', so the human-judgment value (ruling it exempt) still holds. Worth a one-line tightening but not disqualifying.

Computed contrast of the flourish over the brightest scene pixel (#c9cdbf) is ~1.17:1, slightly below the doc's stated '1.4-2.0:1' floor; this only strengthens the 'fails if in scope' claim, so it is a precision nit not an error.

Borderline automated-detectability: a plain ratio checker (axe-core) does NOT exempt large text from contrast checks — it applies the 3:1 large-text bar, and 2.52 < 3, so axe WOULD already flag this element as a contrast violation. The genuinely human-only part is the decorative-vs-informative SCOPE judgment, not the ratio itself; the failing ratio is mechanically catchable, which weakens the 'tools miss it' framing in the .md (lines 37-44) and HTML comment (lines 90-100).

Minor: the .md/HTML comment claim that scanners 'down-weight large text' and therefore miss it is misleading — mainstream scanners apply the 3:1 large-text threshold and still fail 2.52:1; they would not silently pass it.

Minor framing weakness (not a defect): the divider is aria-hidden="true", and the strongest contrast checker (axe-core's color-contrast rule) excludes elements hidden from AT, so axe would already correctly NOT fail this page. The doc's 'tools false-positive' claim only holds for naive ratio scanners that read visible text and ignore aria-hidden; the genuine human-judgment content is distinguishing this decorative repeated word from a meaningful one (the case-01 pair), not merely computing 1.5:1.

The .md attribute tuple references case-01 as 'DRAFT' (the meaningful repeated-word counterpart); I did not verify case-01 exists/has the opposite ruling, so the claimed structural-pair contrast is asserted but unverified here.

The ACTUAL file (case-05.html) is a transit ticket whose meaningful text is platform code 'B7' (.platform .code), color #c8cdca over an inline-SVG floorplan image. Both quotes are legitimately verbatim in their respective sources — the trusted-tester quote 'Purely decorative and not meaningful (no functionality)' is verbatim at line 12 — but the cross-file citation inconsistency is worth flagging.

The measured 2.07:1 fails both, so the 'failed' outcome is correct regardless, but the cited threshold is technically wrong for this size/weight.

Partial automated detectability: a stock contrast scanner (axe/Lighthouse/WAVE) DOES compute and flag 2.07:1 on this text node (the page itself admits this, HTML lines 73-85). The human judgment is required to UPHOLD the flag against the 'logos are exempt' defense, not to FIND the low contrast. So the element is not invisible to tooling; the dispositive reasoning (exemption erosion via UI-component function) is the human part.
